task_title: ATC Clearances, Communications and Transponder Use
objective: By the end of this lesson you can say when you must follow an ATC clearance or instruction and when you may deviate, talk to ATC with standard phraseology, and set the right transponder code and mode for normal flight, emergencies and lost communications.
why: Most ATC trouble starts with a missed word, a wrong number or a clearance accepted without thinking. The PIC, not the controller, stays the final authority for the flight. The regulatory review guide in AC 61-98E, used for flight reviews, lists authority (91.3), ATC instructions (91.123), the transponder rule (91.215), radio communications and clearances [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]] [[15:41|AC 61-98E App E]].

prereading.what: The two rules that set your authority and your duty to follow ATC. Short: read every word.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.3 and 91.123

prereading.what: What a clearance is and is not, readbacks, amended clearances, and how to fly climbs, descents and headings ATC gives you.
prereading.label: AIM 4-4-1 to 4-4-10

prereading.what: Radio technique, contact procedures, call signs, the phonetic alphabet, numbers and time, and radio failure at a tower.
prereading.label: AIM 4-2-1 to 4-2-14

prereading.what: How to operate the transponder and ADS-B Out on the ground and in the air, code changes, and every SQUAWK instruction.
prereading.label: AIM 4-1-20

prereading.what: MAYDAY and PAN-PAN, the distress message, and which code to squawk in an emergency.
prereading.label: AIM 6-3-1 to 6-3-2

prereading.what: Two-way radio failure: who decides if it is an emergency, the 91.185 rules, and code 7600.
prereading.label: AIM 6-4-1 to 6-4-2

prereading.what: The FAA English language standard every certificated pilot must keep meeting, and how it is checked at a flight review.
prereading.label: AC 60-28B paras 1 to 6

warmup: Think first: Approach tells you, "Turn left heading two seven zero, descend and maintain two thousand five hundred." Ahead on that heading is a cloud bank, and 2,500 ft would put you close to a ridge. You are VFR. Do you have to fly it? What exactly would you say back?

key_terms.def: An authorization from ATC, to prevent collisions between known aircraft, to proceed under stated conditions in controlled airspace. It never authorizes breaking a rule or an unsafe operation.
A directive from ATC that tells you to take a specific action, such as "turn left heading two five zero" or "go around."
Under 91.3(a) the PIC is directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft.
A changed clearance. You may ask for one any time the issued clearance would break a rule or put you in danger.
Repeating parts of a clearance or instruction back to ATC, with your call sign, so both sides can check the numbers.
The standard word that says you cannot comply with an instruction, request or clearance.
Serious or imminent danger that needs immediate help. MAYDAY has absolute priority on the frequency.
A safety concern that needs timely but not immediate help; a possible distress.
ATC's word for a transponder code or function, as in "squawk four five two one" or "squawk VFR."
The transponder feature that sends your pressure altitude, in 100 ft steps, to ATC and to TCAS and ADS-B In users.
A button that makes your target stand out on the controller's display. Press it only when ATC asks.
The FAA Aviation English Language Standard: be able to communicate in English with ATC and others, at no less than ICAO Operational Level 4.

callout.text: 91.3: the PIC is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft. In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from any rule of part 91 to the extent required to meet it, and must send a written report if the Administrator asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

head: Paragraph of 91.123
What it says
rows: (a) Clearances

Once you have a clearance, do not deviate unless you get an amended clearance, an emergency exists, or you are following a TCAS resolution advisory. If you are uncertain of a clearance, ask ATC right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]
(b) Instructions
Except in an emergency, do not operate contrary to an ATC instruction in an area where ATC is exercised [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]]
(c) Tell ATC
If you deviate for an emergency or a TCAS RA, notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]
(d) Priority report
If ATC gave you priority in an emergency, even with no rule broken, send a detailed report within 48 hours to that facility's manager if ATC asks [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]]

body.p: A clearance is based on known traffic and known airport conditions. It is not authorization to deviate from any rule, regulation or minimum altitude, or to fly unsafely [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1a]]. The AIM applies the no-deviation rule to clearances under both visual and instrument flight rules [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10a]]. Application: for a VFR pilot that includes a Class B clearance or a landing clearance.

callout.text: Clearance = permission ("cleared to..."). Instruction = do this now ("turn left heading...", "go around") [[34:303|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]] [[34:314|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]. Both bind you, and neither overrides 91.3.

Watch out: "ATC told me to" does not end your duty. If a clearance would make you break a rule, or in your opinion put the aircraft in jeopardy, it is your job to request an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1b]].

check.q: You deviated from a clearance in an emergency. What must you do, and when?
check.a: Notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]] and get an amended clearance [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10f]]. A written report goes to the Administrator only if requested [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]].

body.p: It is your responsibility to accept or refuse a clearance [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7c]]. Once you accept it, ATC expects you to carry it out on receipt. "IMMEDIATELY" means fast compliance is needed for safety [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10a]]. With a heading or turn, start the turn promptly, finish it, and hold the new heading [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10b]].

bullets: Read back altitudes, altitude restrictions, vectors and runway assignments, in the order given, with your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b1-2]].
Do not read back altitudes from charted procedures unless the controller states them [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b3]].
Include left, right or center when you read back a runway [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b4]].
Under IFR, write the clearance down [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7a]].

head: ATC says
What you do
rows: "Descend and maintain (altitude)"
Start down promptly at an optimum rate to 1,000 ft above the altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm. Tell ATC if you cannot do at least 500 fpm, or if you must level off early [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10d]]
"At pilot's discretion"
Start when you like, at any rate, and level off on the way if you wish. Once you leave an altitude, you may not go back to it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10c]]
"Expedite"
About your best rate, without unusual handling [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10i]]. If the altitude is later restated without "expedite," the expedite is canceled [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10i]]
A new clearance that leaves out an old restriction
The last clearance wins. If the altitude to maintain is changed or restated and earlier altitude restrictions are left out, they are canceled [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10g]]

body.p: You may always request a different clearance if you have information that makes another plan more practical, or if your equipment cannot comply [[33:277|AIM 4-4-4c]]. If you want something different, such as another runway or a 360 for spacing, tell ATC, and cooperate so you do not upset the traffic flow [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1b]].

check.q: ATC says "descend at pilot's discretion, maintain four thousand." You leave 7,000 and level at 6,000 for a while. May you climb back to 7,000 without asking?
check.a: No. Once you vacate an altitude under pilot's discretion you may not return to it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10c]].

body.p: The single most important thought in pilot-controller communication is understanding. Keep it brief, but use whatever words are needed to get the message across [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1b]]. Jargon, chatter and "CB" slang have no place on the frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1c]].

bullets: Listen before you transmit. After a frequency change, pause and listen [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2a]].
Think before you key the mike. Jot down anything long [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2b]].
Mike close to your lips; after pressing the button, a slight pause so the first word goes out; normal tone [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2c]].
After you release the button, wait a few seconds before calling again [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2d]].
Silence for too long? Check volume and frequency, and make sure your mike is not stuck in transmit [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2e]].
Higher altitude increases VHF line-of-sight range [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2f]].

body.p: A headset with a boom microphone is recommended. A hand mike and the cabin speaker add the distraction of reaching for the mike [[23:53|IFH 2-2]]. Headphones put the signal right at your ears, so cockpit noise does not hide what ATC says [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]. If ATC assigns a frequency your radio cannot select, ask for another one [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

callout.text: Keep listening even when the call is not for you. The AIM asks pilots to monitor the frequency for traffic conflicts, especially on an active runway or on final approach [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1b]].

check.q: The frequency has been dead quiet for several minutes in busy airspace. What three things does the AIM tell you to check?
check.a: Your volume, your frequency, and that your microphone is not stuck in the transmit position [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2e]].

body.p: Initial contact is your first call to a facility, or to a new controller in it. Say the facility name, your full call sign, your position if you are on the airport surface, then the type of message or a short request, and "over" if needed [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a1]]. Adding your position or altitude and "information Charlie received" saves airtime [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a3]].

head: Facility
Call it
rows: Tower
"Augusta Tower" [[33:231|AIM 4-2-6]]
Ground control
"Miami Ground" [[33:231|AIM 4-2-6]]
Approach or departure control
"Oklahoma City Approach", "St. Louis Departure" [[33:231|AIM 4-2-6]]
ARTCC
"Washington Center" [[33:231|AIM 4-2-6]]
Flight service station
"Chicago Radio" [[33:231|AIM 4-2-6]]

bullets: Acknowledge every callup and clearance with your call sign, at the start or end, plus "wilco," "roger," "affirmative," "negative" or another fitting remark [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3c]].
Acknowledge frequency changes. Silent switching leaves ATC unable to tell whether you heard it or lost your radio [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d1]].
Change frequency as soon as possible, unless told to change at a time, fix or altitude [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3e]].
Leaving an area while getting traffic advisories? Tell ATC and terminate contact [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3c]].

body.p: Civil pilots say the type, model or manufacturer, then the registration; when the type is said, drop the "N": "Aztec Two Four Six Four Alpha" [[33:230|AIM 4-2-4a3]]. Never abbreviate on initial contact, or when similar call signs are on frequency. ATC may start using the prefix and last three characters after contact is made; then you may too [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a1-2]].

callout.text: Watch out: improper call sign use can lead a pilot to fly a clearance meant for someone else. If you doubt that a clearance was yours, say "verify clearance for" and your full call sign [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a]].

check.q: Approach told you "Contact Center on one two eight point three five." Why must you acknowledge before you switch?
check.a: Without the acknowledgement the controller cannot tell whether you got the instruction or had a radio failure [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d1]].

chunks.title: Phraseology: words, letters, numbers and English

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Roger
I received all of your last transmission. Not an answer to a yes or no question [[34:407|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]
Wilco
I received your message, understand it, and will comply [[34:445|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]
Affirmative / Negative
Yes / No, permission not granted, or that is not correct [[34:302|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]] [[34:385|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]
Unable
I cannot comply with that instruction, request or clearance [[34:436|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]
Say again
Repeat your last transmission, often naming the part you missed [[34:413|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]
Read back
Repeat my message back to me [[34:404|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]

bullets: Use the phonetic alphabet for your call sign on initial contact, and for single letters and hard words when reception is poor [[33:232|AIM 4-2-7]].
Round hundreds and thousands up to 9,900: "four thousand five hundred." Above 9,900, split the digits before "thousand": "one three thousand five hundred" [[33:233|AIM 4-2-8a-b]].
Other numbers digit by digit; a frequency's decimal is "point" [[33:233|AIM 4-2-8d-e]].
Headings, courses and winds are magnetic, three digits; add "true" when it is true [[33:233|AIM 4-2-10]].
Speeds: digits then "knots" [[33:234|AIM 4-2-11]]. Time: UTC ("Zulu"); say "local" for local time [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12a]].

callout.text: Every certificated pilot should be able to communicate in English with ATC, pilots and others preparing and operating the aircraft, at no less than ICAO Operational Level 4 [[10:1|AC 60-28B para 1.1]] [[10:2|AC 60-28B para 3]]. The person giving a flight review should evaluate it [[10:4|AC 60-28B para 6]], and should not sign off a flight review for a pilot who does not meet it [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.3]].

body.p: AC 61-98E links poor radio skills to runway incursions, and tells pilots to meet the English standard, use correct pilot/controller terms and a proper voice cadence [[15:16|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.1]].

check.q: ATC asks, "Do you have the airport in sight?" You do. Why is "Roger" the wrong answer?
check.a: Roger only means you received the transmission and is not used to answer a yes or no question [[34:407|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]. Say "affirmative" or report the airport in sight.

chunks.title: Using the transponder in normal flight

callout.text: 91.215(c): in the 91.215(b) airspace and in all controlled airspace, if your aircraft has an operable transponder, operate it, including Mode C if installed, on the appropriate code or the one ATC assigns, unless ATC directs otherwise [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]]. (Where a transponder is required at all is in Area III, Task A.)

bullets: On the ground: altitude reporting mode and ADS-B Out on any time you are on the movement area, taxiways and runways included. STBY or OFF at the parking spot [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a3]].
In the air: on the code assigned, altitude reporting on, in controlled airspace; also on in uncontrolled airspace if practicable [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a4]].
VFR: code 1200 at any altitude unless ATC says otherwise [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5]]. Cancel IFR en route? Set the transponder for VFR [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a6]].
Other VFR codes exist: gliders 1202, firefighting 1255, authorized search and rescue 1277, formation lead 1203 [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5]].
On initial contact, report your exact altitude to the nearest 100 ft so ATC can verify your Mode C [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20c3]].
IDENT only when ATC asks [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20d]]. It is good practice to say that you changed the code or pressed ident [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

head: ATC says
You do
rows: SQUAWK (code)
Set that code, altitude reporting on [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g1]]
SQUAWK (code) AND IDENT
Set the code and press IDENT [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g3]]
SQUAWK STANDBY / SQUAWK NORMAL
Switch to standby / back to normal on the code you had [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g4-5]]
STOP ALTITUDE SQUAWK
Turn off altitude reporting only [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g7]]
STOP SQUAWK
Stop transponder and ADS-B Out transmissions [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g8]]
SQUAWK VFR
Code 1200 or other VFR code, altitude reporting on [[33:225|AIM 4-1-20g10]]

callout.text: "Stop altitude squawk, altitude differs by 300 feet" may mean bad altitude data or a wrong altimeter setting. The encoder is preset to standard pressure, so your Kollsman setting does not change what ATC sees, but a wrong setting does put you at the wrong true altitude. Check your altimeter [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20c2]] [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

check.q: You are taxiing at a towered airport. Where should the transponder be?
check.a: In the altitude reporting mode, with ADS-B Out on, whenever you are on the movement area; STBY or OFF only at the parking spot [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a3]].

head: Code
Meaning and when
rows: VFR, unless ATC assigns another code [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5]]
Hijack: "I am being hijacked/forced to a new destination." ATC never assigns it unless you first report unlawful interference; refuse it otherwise [[34:52|AIM 6-3-4b]]
Loss of two-way radio communications [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]]
Distress or urgency, when you want to alert radar and cannot reach ATC on your code. Also if intercepted, unless ATC says otherwise [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2a]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]] [[34:22|AIM 5-6-13d3]]
Never, in a civil aircraft: military interceptor use only [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e2]]

callout.text: Already talking to ATC on an assigned code when trouble starts? Keep that code and Mode C unless told otherwise. Go to 7700 if you cannot quickly establish communications [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]].

body.p: A 7600 squawk makes the data block flash RDOF, radio failure, on the controller's screen [[29:107|IPH 2-47]]. 7700 normally sets off an alarm at all control positions, but you may be outside radar coverage, so keep squawking and keep trying the radio [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2b]]. Transponders tied to ADS-B set the matching emergency status on their own when you enter 7500, 7600 or 7700 [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7c5]].

callout.text: Watch out when you change codes: do not pass through 7500, 7600 or 7700, which trips false alarms. From 2700 to 7200, go 2200 first, then 7200, not 7700 then 7200 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]].

body.p: If you squawk 7500 by mistake, ATC will ask you to verify it. Say in the clear that you are not being subjected to unlawful interference; ATC will then have you check and correct the code [[34:52|AIM 6-3-4c]].

check.q: You are talking to approach on code 4521 when your oil pressure starts to drop. Do you switch to 7700?
check.a: Not unless told to. In radio contact, keep the assigned code and Mode C; use 7700 if you cannot quickly establish communications [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]].

body.p: Start a distress call with MAYDAY, an urgency call with PAN-PAN, preferably three times [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c]]. MAYDAY has absolute priority and silences the frequency; PAN-PAN has priority over everything but distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1d]]. Use the frequency you are on; 121.5 MHz is there if needed, but it is line of sight [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1e,h]].

bullets: Climb if you can, for better radio and radar coverage, but no unauthorized climb or descent in IFR conditions in controlled airspace except as 91.3(b) permits [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2a1]].

Message, as much as needed: MAYDAY or PAN-PAN; station; call sign and type; the problem; weather; intentions and request; position and heading; altitude; fuel remaining in minutes; people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]].
Then comply with ATC, ask when unsure, and say so if you cannot comply. Do not change frequency unless you must [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2b]].

callout.text: Radio failure: whether it is an emergency depends on the circumstances, and the pilot decides [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1b]]. Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]]. Under IFR in VFR conditions, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]]; "as soon as practicable" does not mean "as soon as possible" [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1c2]].

head: VFR radio failure, towered airport
What to do
rows: Rule

You may land if weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you receive a clearance to land. This is 91.126(d) at a towered airport in Class G and 91.129(d)(2) in Class D; Class C and B operations must also comply with 91.129 [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]] [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]] [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(a)]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)]]
Receiver out

Stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you see the traffic flow, then call the tower with type, position, altitude and intention to land, and ask for light signals. Report 3 to 5 miles out and join the pattern [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a1]]
Transmitter out

Stay outside or above until you see the flow, join the pattern, monitor tower and watch for light signals. Daytime, rock your wings to acknowledge; at night, blink the landing or nav lights [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]]
Both out
Same, and keep visual contact with the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]]

callout.text: Lost the radio on the ground? Try to get it fixed. If you cannot, phone the tower and ask to depart without two-way radio [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13b]].

check.q: Your fuel is 12 gallons at 8 gallons per hour. How does the AIM want fuel stated in a distress message?

chunks.title: Risk: accepting a clearance that puts you in danger

body.p: ATC builds clearances to keep known aircraft apart [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1a]]. ATC may not know your cloud clearance, the terrain right in front of you, or what your airplane can do. Those stay yours, so "unable" is a correct answer [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7c]] [[34:436|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]].

head: Trap
What the sources say
rows: Assigned heading or altitude in Class B leads into cloud, terrain or wake
Tell approach and get a revised clearance or instruction [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e3]]
VFR pilot in trouble being vectored

Radar help is advisory; it does not authorize you to break a rule. A noninstrument pilot should pick the VFR option, and if VFR is not possible, say so, state the lack of an instrument rating and declare distress [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1a-b]]
Assigned altitude seems too low
Query the controller before descending [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]
Picking up IFR below the MEA
You own terrain and obstruction clearance until you reach the minimum IFR altitude; tell ATC if you cannot keep it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-9]]
Special VFR
The pilot is responsible for obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6c]]
Hearing a clearance meant for a similar call sign
Do not act until the call sign is complete and clearly yours [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a2]]

callout.text: Say it short: "Unable, (reason), request (what you can do)." The AIM expects you to request an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1b]], and you may request a different one if equipment limits forbid compliance [[33:277|AIM 4-4-4c]]. If time is short and you must deviate for safety, 91.3(b) and 91.123(a) cover an emergency; tell ATC as soon as possible [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]].

check.q: In Class B, approach assigns 3,500 ft, which would put you into a cloud layer. You are VFR. What do you do?
check.a: Tell approach and get a revised clearance or instruction; the program does not relieve you of the 91.155 weather minimums [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e3]]. "Unable, clouds at three thousand five hundred, request three thousand."

chunks.title: Fly it: respond to ATC and to an equipment failure

body.p: **For each call: hear it, decide if it is safe and legal, then answer with the numbers and your call sign.**

head: ATC or the airplane
A good response
rows: "Cessna Four Five Kilo, squawk five three two one and ident."
Set 5321 without passing through 7500, 7600 or 7700, press IDENT once [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]] [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g3]]. "Five three two one, Cessna Four Five Kilo."
"Cessna Four Five Kilo, turn right heading one two zero, climb and maintain five thousand five hundred."
Turn promptly and read back in the same order: "Right one two zero, climb and maintain five thousand five hundred, Cessna Four Five Kilo" [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b1-2]] [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10b]]
That heading points into a cloud
"Unable heading one two zero, clouds. Request one five zero." Ask for an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1b]]
You are not sure whether the call was for you
"Verify clearance for Cessna Four Five Kilo" [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a2]]. If unsure what it means, ask at once [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]
"Stop altitude squawk, altitude differs by three hundred feet."
Turn off altitude reporting, check the altimeter setting [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20c2]]
Radios quiet, then nothing works

Check volume, frequency and a stuck mike [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2e]]. Try the last frequency, an FSS, and 121.5 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-3a]] [[34:55|AIM 6-4-3b]] [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1h]]. Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]]
Engine running rough, in contact with ATC

Keep the assigned code [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]]. "PAN-PAN" (or MAYDAY) three times, station, call sign and type, problem, weather, intentions and request, position and heading, altitude, fuel in minutes, people on board [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]]

callout.text: The AC 61-98E regulatory review guide lists authority (91.3), radio communications (AIM 4-2 and the Pilot/Controller Glossary) and clearances (AIM 4-4) [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]] [[15:41|AC 61-98E App E]]. Bring the AIM 4-1-20g squawk list on a kneeboard card.

check.q: "Cessna Four Five Kilo, descend and maintain three thousand, contact approach one two five point three five." What is a complete readback?
check.a: "Descend and maintain three thousand, one two five point three five, Cessna Four Five Kilo." Read back the altitude, acknowledge the frequency change, and include your call sign [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b1]] [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d1]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Answering a yes or no question with "roger"
Say "affirmative" or "negative" [[34:407|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]
Reading back without a call sign
Include your call sign in every readback [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b1]]
Flying a clearance you were not sure of
Ask right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]
Accepting a heading or altitude into cloud or terrain
"Unable," and request an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1b]]
Switching frequencies silently
Acknowledge first [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d1]]
Pressing IDENT unasked, or dialing through 7700
IDENT only on request; avoid 7500, 7600 and 7700 when changing codes [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20d-e]]
Transponder in standby while taxiing
Altitude mode on the whole movement area [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a3]]
Forgetting to tell ATC after an emergency deviation
Notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]

check.q: Why is pressing IDENT "just to help" a mistake?
check.a: Transponder and ADS-B Out are operated only as ATC specifies; activate IDENT only when ATC requests it [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20d]].

f1.caption: IFH Figure 2-1 (part). Typical navigation/communication installation, with the side labels cropped off (IFH 2-2).
f1.alt: A radio stack: two com transceivers on the left and two nav receivers on the right, each showing USE and STBY frequencies; an ADF; a GPS showing position, groundspeed and track; and at the bottom a KT 70 transponder with an IDT button, code 1200 in the window, four code knobs and a mode knob with OFF, SBY, ON, ALT and TST positions.

f2.caption: IFH Figure 2-3. Boom microphone, headset, and push-to-talk switch (IFH 2-3).
f2.alt: A pilot headset with a boom microphone and two plugs, and below it a push-to-talk switch on a strap with its coiled cord.

f3.caption: PHAK Figure 14-41. Phonetic alphabet (PHAK 14-24).
f3.alt: Table of letters A to Z and digits 1 to 0 with Morse code, the telephony word (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie and so on) and the pronunciation, such as NIN-ER for nine and TREE for three.

f4.caption: IFH Figure 2-9 (top image). An ARTS III display as seen by controllers, with its symbols explained (IFH 2-8).
f4.alt: A round radar display titled Academy Planned View Display. Callouts point to tracked targets with data blocks showing call sign, altitude and speed, untracked targets with Mode C, a tracked primary target, a system data area, tabular lists and a readout area.

f5.caption: IPH Figure 2-69. Two-way radio communications failure transponder code (IPH 2-47).
f5.alt: A dark radar screen with the yellow-green data block 7600 over RDOF next to a target, and a note that when an aircraft squawks 7600 the data block flashes RDOF, radio failure, to alert the controller.

f6.caption: IFH Figure 2-8. Minimum vectoring altitude (MVA) chart (IFH 2-6).
f6.alt: A circular chart around a radar antenna, split into sectors by bearing lines. Red boxes show minimum vectoring altitudes such as 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 3500 and 5000, with green range rings at 5 to 30 miles and brown obstruction symbols of 5500 and 3000 that need extra clearance.

scenario.title: Flight following into a busy Class D
scenario.setup: You fly a Cessna 172, call sign Cessna Four Five Kilo, VFR from a nontowered field to a towered Class D airport 60 NM away. You call approach for flight following. Clouds are scattered at 3,500 ft over hills that rise to 2,000 ft MSL. You are not instrument rated.

questions.q: What do you say on initial contact with approach?
questions.a: Facility, full call sign, then the request, with position and altitude: "Columbus Approach, Cessna Four Five Kilo, request VFR traffic advisories, ten south of Bolton, three thousand five hundred" [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a1, a3]]. Use the phonetic alphabet for the call sign on initial contact [[33:232|AIM 4-2-7]].

questions.q: Approach says "Squawk four six one two and ident." What do you do, and what code were you on before?
questions.a: You were on 1200, the VFR code [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5]]. Set 4612 with altitude reporting on and press IDENT once [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g3]].

questions.q: Approach: "Turn left heading two seven zero, descend and maintain two thousand." That heading crosses the hills, which reach 2,000 ft. Must you comply?
questions.a: No. A clearance or instruction never authorizes an unsafe operation, and the PIC is the final authority [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1a-b]] [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]]. Say "unable" and request an amended clearance, such as three thousand [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1b]]. When compliance is likely to compromise terrain clearance or weather minimums, the AIM says to advise approach and get a revised clearance or instruction [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e3]].

questions.q: Ten miles from the Class D, the radio goes silent. Checking shows no stuck mike and the volume is up. What code, and what next?
questions.a: Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]]. Stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you see the traffic flow, join the pattern and watch the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a]].

questions.q: May you land there without talking to the tower?
questions.a: Yes, if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you get a clearance to land, by light signal [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]]. A steady green in flight means cleared to land [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]].

questions.q: In the pattern the tower flashes a light at you in daylight. How do you acknowledge with no transmitter?
questions.a: Rock your wings. At night you would blink the landing or navigation lights [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]].

skills.do: Given ATC calls and failures, answer each with correct phraseology and a readback that includes the call sign; say "unable" to any clearance that would break a rule or put the airplane in danger; set the correct transponder code and mode for VFR, an assigned code, IDENT, an emergency and lost communications; and fly the radio failure procedure at a towered airport.
skills.practice: With a reviewer playing ATC, run ten calls from the table in the Fly it chunk, including at least one unsafe instruction. Practice code changes on the real transponder on the ground, never dialing through 7500, 7600 or 7700 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]]. Rehearse a distress message in AIM order [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]] and the receiver-out and transmitter-out arrivals at a tower [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]]. The AC 61-98E regulatory review guide lists radio communications and clearances [[15:41|AC 61-98E App E]].

quiz.q: Under 91.123(a), which of these is NOT a reason you may deviate from an ATC clearance?
options: An emergency exists
You think another route would be faster
You are following a TCAS resolution advisory
You received an amended clearance
quiz.why: You may deviate only with an amended clearance, in an emergency, or for a TCAS RA [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. For a better route, request a different clearance [[33:277|AIM 4-4-4c]].

quiz.q: You are uncertain of an ATC clearance. What does 91.123(a) require?
options: Immediately request clarification from ATC
Fly what you think it meant and confirm later
Hold your present heading and altitude until ATC calls
Squawk 7600
quiz.why: When a pilot is uncertain of a clearance, that pilot shall immediately request clarification from ATC [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

quiz.q: Approach says, "Traffic, two o'clock, three miles, eastbound, altitude indicates four thousand five hundred." You look but cannot see it. What is the best reply?
options: "Negative contact, Cessna Four Five Kilo"
"Roger, Cessna Four Five Kilo"
"Unable, Cessna Four Five Kilo"
"Wilco, Cessna Four Five Kilo"
quiz.why: "Negative contact" tells ATC that previously issued traffic is not in sight [[34:385|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]. Roger only means you received the call [[34:407|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]; unable means you cannot comply [[34:436|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]].

quiz.q: When may you shorten your call sign to "Cessna Four Five Kilo"?
options: On every call including the first one, as long as the controller can still understand you
On initial contact whenever the frequency is busy and you need to keep the call short
After contact is made and ATC abbreviates it, if no similar call signs are around
Never; the pilot must always use the full call sign, even after ATC abbreviates it
quiz.why: Never abbreviate on initial contact or with similar call signs on frequency. ATC may start the abbreviation after contact; then the pilot may use it [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a1-2]].

quiz.q: How do you say 10,500 ft on the radio?
options: One zero thousand five hundred
Ten thousand five hundred
One zero five zero zero
Flight level one zero five
quiz.why: Below 18,000 ft MSL, say the separate digits of the thousands plus the hundreds [[33:233|AIM 4-2-9a]]; above 9,900, separate the digits before "thousand" [[33:233|AIM 4-2-8b]].

quiz.q: On initial contact with approach, how should you state your altitude?
options: Rounded to the nearest 500 ft
Say "Mode C on" instead of an altitude
Exact altitude to the nearest 100 ft
As a flight level
quiz.why: Report exact altitude to the nearest hundred foot increment on initial contact, so ATC can use your Mode C readout for separation [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20c3]].

quiz.q: Your transponder works and you fly VFR in Class E airspace, not talking to ATC. What does 91.215(c) require?
options: Nothing; the transponder may stay off in Class E
Transponder on in standby, since ATC isn't working you
Transponder on with Mode C, on the appropriate code
Transponder on only above 10,000 ft MSL, off below
quiz.why: In all controlled airspace, an aircraft with an operable transponder must operate it, including Mode C if installed, on the appropriate code or as assigned [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]]. For VFR that is 1200 [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5]].

quiz.q: ATC said "squawk standby" a few minutes ago. Now you hear "squawk normal." What do you do?
options: Set 1200, since standby cleared your assigned code
Set 7600, since ATC just confirmed a radio failure
Turn the transponder off and on to reset it
Resume normal operation on the code you had before standby
quiz.why: SQUAWK NORMAL means resume normal transponder/ADS-B operation on the previously assigned code [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g5]]. The "low or normal sensitivity" meaning in PHAK Figure 14-43 is older wording [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]].

quiz.q: Which word starts an urgency call?
options: MAYDAY
PAN-PAN
SECURITY
EMERGENCY
quiz.why: MAYDAY is for distress and PAN-PAN for urgency, preferably said three times [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c]].

takeaways: The PIC is the final authority (91.3). A clearance never lets you break a rule or fly unsafely.
Deviate from a clearance only with an amended clearance, in an emergency or for a TCAS RA, then tell ATC as soon as possible.
Not sure? Ask at once. Unsafe? Say "unable" and request what you can do.
Read back altitudes, headings and runways with your call sign; acknowledge every frequency change.
Roger is not yes. Wilco means you will comply.
1200 VFR, 7500 hijack, 7600 radio failure, 7700 emergency, never 7777. Keep an assigned code while you are talking to ATC.
Transponder in altitude mode whenever you are on the movement area or in controlled airspace; IDENT only when asked.
cfi_notes: Run this as a role play: you are ATC, the pilot answers. Slip in one unsafe instruction and one call for a similar call sign, and see whether the pilot says "unable" or "verify clearance for" [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a2]].
AIM 6-4-1b says 91.3(b) allows deviation from any rule in Subparts A and B; the regulation itself says "any rule of this part" [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1b]] [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. Teach the CFR wording.

PHAK Figure 14-43 is older than the AIM: it defines "SQUAWK Low/Normal" as transponder sensitivity, "STOP SQUAWK" as switching the transponder off, and has no ADS-B. AIM 4-1-20g5 defines SQUAWK NORMAL as resuming normal transponder/ADS-B operation on the previously assigned code, and g8 STOP SQUAWK as stopping transponder and ADS-B Out transmissions [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]] [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g5, g8]]. Teach the AIM list.

IFH 2-3 says altitude reporting is required only in Class B, Class C and the 30-mile Class B area, and that it "should" be on elsewhere. That is incomplete. 91.215(b) and AIM 4-1-20f2 also list Class A, above the Class B and C ceilings, and Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL; and 91.215(c) and AIM 4-1-20a4 require Mode C on, if installed, in all controlled airspace [[23:54|IFH 2-3]] [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)-(c)]] [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a4]] [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f2]]. Teach the CFR and AIM.

Airline and turbine pilots will know readbacks well; spend their time on 91.123(d) (48 hour report if requested), on 4-4-10g (the last clearance cancels restrictions it leaves out) and on the expedite rule [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]] [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10g]] [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10i]].

English: AC 61-98E says not to sign off a flight review when the pilot does not meet the English standard; log the training received and notify the Flight Standards office [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.3]]. AC 60-28B gives the six ICAO Level 4 areas to listen for [[10:2|AC 60-28B para 4.1]] [[10:3|AC 60-28B para 4.1]].

Point out the difference between an IFR comm failure (91.185) and a VFR one at a tower (91.126(d), 91.129(d), AIM 4-2-13). Many refresher pilots mix them up [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185]] [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)]].
This Task focuses on using the transponder. Where it is required and the ATC deviation process were taught in Area III, Task A; send the pilot back there if those come up.
gaps: 91.123(b) applies "in an area in which air traffic control is exercised." Whether that includes, for example, Class G flight following is a legal interpretation; FAA interpretations are not in the sources.
The sources give no fixed wording for "unable." The short format in this lesson is application, built from the glossary meaning and AIM 4-4-1b.
How to change codes, find the ALT position or set the standby frequency on a given radio or transponder comes from its manual or the POH/AFM, not from these sources.
Light gun signals and taxi and hold short phraseology are only touched on here; they are in Area IV, Task B.
Full IFR lost communication procedures (route, altitude and when to leave the clearance limit under 91.185(c)) are left to Area V.

activities.title: True or false: clearances and authority
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: If ATC clears you to do something, that clearance lets you break a regulation.
cards.why: False. A clearance is not authorization to deviate from any rule, regulation or minimum altitude [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1a]].

cards.s: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from any rule of part 91 to the extent needed.
After any 91.3(b) deviation, you must file a written report within 48 hours even if no one asks.
cards.why: False. The written report goes to the Administrator on request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]]. The 48 hour report is for priority handling, and only if ATC requests it [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].

cards.s: You should read back altitudes, vectors and runway assignments.
cards.why: True, as a mutual check, with your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]].

cards.s: Always read back the altitudes printed on a departure procedure chart.
cards.why: False. Do not read back charted procedure altitudes unless the controller states them [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b3]].

cards.s: When a new clearance conflicts with an earlier one, the last clearance takes precedence.

activities.title: Build an initial call on the ramp
activities.intro: You are on the south ramp and want to taxi for a VFR departure. Use the arrows to put the parts of your first call to ground in order, then tap Check.
steps: Your full aircraft identification: "Cessna Three One Six Zero Foxtrot"
Your position on the airport: "south ramp"
Your request: "taxi for VFR departure, with information Bravo"
activities.why: Initial contact: facility name, full call sign, position when on the airport surface, the type of message or short request, then "over" if required [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a1]]. Adding the ATIS code helps cut frequency congestion [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a3]].

activities.title: Say what you mean
activities.intro: Tap a word, then its meaning.

pairs.r: I received all of your last transmission
No, or that is not correct

activities.title: Find it on the radio stack
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin. Pins 1 and 2 are on the top left radio, pin 3 on the top right radio, and pins 4 to 6 on the bottom unit.

pins.label: Active com frequency you talk on
Standby com frequency set up next
Mode knob: set ALT for altitude reporting

activities.title: Which code?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then the code it calls for.

items.t: Flying VFR at 9,500 ft, no code assigned by ATC
You cancel IFR en route and ATC gives no new code
A person on board threatens you and forces a new destination
You cannot transmit or receive on any radio
Engine failure and you cannot quickly reach ATC
A military jet intercepts you and ATC has given no other instruction

activities.why: 1200 VFR [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5-6]]; 7500 hijack [[34:52|AIM 6-3-4b]]; 7600 radio failure [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]]; 7700 when unable to reach ATC [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]] or intercepted [[34:22|AIM 5-6-13d3]]; 7777 is reserved for military interceptors [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e2]].

activities.title: Numbers on the radio
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You plan to depart at 1430 Eastern Daylight Time. What is that in UTC (hhmm, as a number)?
items.why: Eastern Standard: add 5 hours; for daylight time subtract 1, so add 4 [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12b]]. 1430 + 4 hours = 1830 UTC.

items.q: ATC gives an expected time of 2215 UTC. What is that in Central Standard Time (hhmm)?
items.why: Central Standard is UTC minus 6 hours (add 6 to go the other way) [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12b]]. 2215 - 6 hours = 1615 CST.

items.q: In a distress message, you have 22 gallons usable and burn 8.8 gallons per hour. What fuel remaining do you report, in minutes?
items.why: The AIM asks for fuel remaining in minutes [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]]. 22 / 8.8 = 2.5 hours x 60 = 150 minutes.

items.q: Each transponder digit runs 0 to 7, and a code has four digits. How many codes are there?
items.why: 8 x 8 x 8 x 8 = 4,096, the number of discrete codes the AIM names [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20b1]] [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]].

items.q: At 9,500 ft you hear "descend and maintain five thousand" with no pilot's discretion. At what altitude should you be down to a 500 to 1,500 fpm rate?
items.why: Descend at an optimum rate to 1,000 ft above the assigned altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10d]]. 5,000 + 1,000 = 6,000 ft.

activities.title: Can I fly this clearance? A hazy afternoon departure
activities.intro: You depart VFR in a Piper Archer, call sign Piper Two One Four Lima, from a Class C airport. Visibility is 6 miles in haze, with a broken layer at 4,000 ft. You are not instrument rated.

steps.s: Departure: "Piper Two One Four Lima, turn right heading three six zero, climb and maintain four thousand five hundred." What do you answer?
options: "Roger, Piper Two One Four Lima. Turning right three six zero, climbing four thousand five hundred, entering the broken layer at four thousand"
Say nothing, turn right to three six zero, and quietly level at 3,500 ft since you cannot climb into the layer
"Unable four thousand five hundred, broken layer at four thousand. Request three thousand five hundred, Piper Two One Four Lima"
"Wilco, Piper Two One Four Lima," then climb to four thousand five hundred and request an IFR clearance once in the clouds
steps.why: A clearance never authorizes unsafe operation or breaking a rule, and it is your job to request an amended one [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1a-b]]. Unable means you cannot comply [[34:436|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]. Leveling off without telling ATC goes against the instruction [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]], and climbing into the layer would break the VFR cloud clearance minimums [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]].

steps.s: "Piper One Four Lima, squawk two seven zero zero." A minute later: "Piper One Four Lima, correction, squawk seven two zero zero." How do you change the code?
options: Turn the first knob from 2 to 7 first, then the second from 7 to 2
Change 2700 to 2200 first, then to 7200
Go to standby, then set 7200
Squawk 7700 briefly to show ATC you got it
steps.why: Avoid passing through 7500, 7600 or 7700: from 2700 to 7200, switch to 2200 then 7200, not 7700 then 7200 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]].

steps.s: A similar call sign, Piper Two One Four Mike, is on the frequency. You hear "...Four Lima... descend and maintain two thousand" partly blocked. What do you do?
options: Descend at once; it sounded like yours
Ignore it
Squawk ident
"Verify clearance for Piper Two One Four Lima"
steps.why: Make sure the identification is complete and clearly yours before acting, and use "verify clearance for" your full call sign when in doubt [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a2]]. If uncertain, ask at once [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

steps.s: The haze thickens and you lose sight of the ground ahead. ATC offers vectors toward your destination, where the weather is worse. A clear airport is 10 miles behind you. What does the AIM say?
options: Choose the course that keeps you in VFR conditions and tell the controller
Accept the vectors; radar guidance makes it legal
Climb above the haze and request an IFR clearance
Keep going toward the destination and hope it improves
steps.why: Radar help is advisory and does not authorize breaking the CFRs. A noninstrument pilot should choose the VFR option over vectors into IFR weather, and keep the controller advised [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1a-b]].

steps.s: Turning back, your radio quits completely. You are 8 miles from the towered airport you left. What now?
options: Enter the pattern at once and land, because no light signals are needed when you are flying VFR in good weather
Squawk 7500 to tell the tower about the radio failure and land straight in without waiting for any signal
Squawk 7777 so the tower knows about the radio failure and can clear you straight in
Squawk 7600, stay outside or above the surface area until you see the flow, then join and land on green
steps.why: 7600 for radio failure [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]]. Remain outside or above the surface area until the flow is known, join the pattern and keep visual contact with the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]]. 91.130(a) makes Class C operations comply with 91.129 [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(a)]], and 91.129(d)(2) lets you land after a VFR radio failure if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you receive a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]]. A steady green to an aircraft in flight means cleared to land [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]].

final_quiz.q: Approach gave you priority for a rough engine, and you landed without breaking any rule. Afterward ATC asks for a report. What do you owe?
options: Nothing, since no rule was broken and you landed safely without any deviation
A detailed report within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility
A written report to the NTSB within 10 days of the event, sent to the regional office
A phone call to the nearest Flight Service station within 24 hours of landing
final_quiz.why: A PIC given priority in an emergency, even without deviating from a rule, submits a detailed report within 48 hours to the facility manager if ATC requests it [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]] [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10f]].

final_quiz.q: ATC: "descend and maintain four thousand," no pilot's discretion. Passing 6,000 you must level off for a minute to slow down. You are not at 10,000 ft MSL or 2,500 ft above an airport. What does the AIM expect?
options: Advise ATC that you are leveling off
Nothing; leveling off is your choice
Squawk standby while level
Ask for pilot's discretion only if ATC calls you
final_quiz.why: Without pilot's discretion, if you must level off at an intermediate altitude, advise ATC. The only exceptions are leveling at 10,000 ft MSL or 2,500 ft above airport elevation for the 91.117 speed limits [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10d]].

final_quiz.q: You were cleared to cross a fix at 6,000 then maintain 4,000. Before the fix ATC says "turn right heading one eight zero, maintain four thousand." What about the 6,000 crossing?
options: Still in effect, because ATC never said to cancel it
You must ask ATC before ignoring it each time
In effect only on an IFR flight plan; canceled for VFR
Canceled, because it was left out when the altitude was restated
final_quiz.why: When the altitude to maintain is changed or restated and earlier altitude restrictions are left out, they are canceled [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10g]] [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10g]].

final_quiz.q: ATC: "Expedite climb to six thousand." Then: "Climb and maintain eight thousand." What rate now?
options: Normal climb; the expedite was canceled when the altitude changed without it
Keep expediting to 8,000, since the earlier expedite instruction was never canceled
Level at 6,000 ft and wait until ATC repeats the expedite before climbing further
Climb at exactly 500 fpm until ATC gives a rate
final_quiz.why: If the altitude is changed or restated without an expedite instruction, the expedite is canceled [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10i]].

final_quiz.q: ATC says "Stop squawk." What do you do?
options: Turn off altitude reporting only and leave the code set
Switch to standby, then back to normal on the same code
Stop transponder and ADS-B Out transmissions
Set code 7600 so ATC knows your radio is out
final_quiz.why: "Stop squawk" means stop transponder and ADS-B Out transmissions [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g8]]. Turning off altitude reporting only is "stop altitude squawk", and standby then normal is "squawk standby" and "squawk normal" [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g7]] [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20g4-5]].

final_quiz.q: You are in contact with approach on code 0425 when smoke appears in the cabin. Which is right?
options: Switch to 7700 at once, then call ATC and tell them what the emergency is
Keep 0425 and Mode C unless told otherwise, and declare the emergency
Switch to 7600 so ATC sees you have a radio problem and clears the airspace
Switch to 1200 to free the discrete code so ATC can reassign it to others
final_quiz.why: When in radio contact, continue squawking the assigned code and Mode C unless instructed otherwise [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]]. Declare with MAYDAY [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c]].

final_quiz.q: You set 7500 by mistake, and ATC asks you to verify your code. What should you do?
options: Say in the clear that you are not subject to unlawful interference, then set the right code
Say nothing; ATC will figure it out
Switch to 7700
Turn the transponder off
final_quiz.why: If not subject to unlawful interference, broadcast that in the clear; the controller will then ask you to verify and correct the code [[34:52|AIM 6-3-4c]].

final_quiz.q: VFR, your receiver fails but the transmitter seems to work. You are 15 miles from your towered destination. What does the AIM say to do first?
options: Fly straight into the Class D surface area and land, watching the tower for a green light signal on final
Stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the flow, then request light signals
Divert to the nearest Class B airport, since radar controllers there can handle a receiver failure
Squawk 7500 and orbit outside the surface area until the tower flashes a light signal at your airplane
final_quiz.why: Receiver inoperative: remain outside or above the Class D surface area until direction and flow of traffic are known, then advise the tower of type, position, altitude and intention to land and request light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a1]].

final_quiz.q: A noninstrument rated pilot in deteriorating weather finds continued VFR flight is no longer possible. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Ask for radar vectors to the destination and keep quiet about your lack of an instrument rating
Squawk 7600 and press on under VFR toward the destination while looking for a hole in the clouds
Tell the controller, state you have no instrument rating, and declare a distress condition
File IFR in the air, since ATC can issue an IFR clearance to any pilot who asks for one
final_quiz.why: If continued VFR is not possible, the noninstrument rated pilot should advise the controller, indicate the lack of an instrument rating, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b2]].

final_quiz.q: Center says, "Cessna Four Five Kilo, at the Bravo intersection contact approach on one two four point six." You acknowledge. When do you change frequency?
options: Right away, to save time
When you can see the airport
Only after Center calls you again
At Bravo, monitoring Center until then
final_quiz.why: Normally change as soon as possible, but when told to change at a time, fix or altitude, monitor the present frequency until you reach it [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3e]].

final_quiz.q: Giving a flight review, a CFI finds the pilot cannot understand routine ATC calls in English. What does AC 61-98E say to do?
options: Sign off the review but add a note about the pilot's English problem in the logbook
Not sign it off; log the training, advise the pilot, and notify Flight Standards
Log a failed flight review in the pilot's logbook and tell the pilot to retake it later
Sign it off if the pilot flew well, since ATC calls are not part of the review itself
final_quiz.why: Do not endorse the review as satisfactory; log only training received, advise the pilot, and notify the responsible Flight Standards office. There is no "failed" flight review entry [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.3]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing out under IFR in VMC, a TCAS resolution advisory tells you to descend, against your clearance. You follow it. What must you do next?
options: Nothing; TCAS deviations need no report
Squawk 7700 for one minute
File a written report within 48 hours
Notify ATC of the deviation as soon as possible
final_quiz.why: A deviation in response to a TCAS RA is allowed, and the pilot must notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a), (c)]] [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1c]].

final_quiz.q: On a busy frequency you want flight following, and you want the controller to know your position and altitude in your first call. Which call fits the AIM best?
options: "Approach, it's me again, the Cessna. I'm northwest of Rome at about seven thousand five hundred."
"Atlanta Center, Duke Four One Romeo, request VFR traffic advisories, over, and nothing else."
"Atlanta Center, Four One Romeo, request VFR traffic advisories, twenty northwest Rome, seven thousand five hundred."
"Atlanta Center, Duke Four One Romeo, request VFR traffic advisories, twenty northwest Rome, seven thousand five hundred."
final_quiz.why: Facility, full call sign, request, and position and altitude in one short call, if reception is reasonably assured [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a1, a3]]. Call signs are not abbreviated on initial contact [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a1]].
